desc:
A binary tree with distinct node values is described by a list of edges, in arbitrary order. Each edge is a triple [parent, child, isLeft]: the node child hangs below the node parent, as its left child if isLeft = 1 and as its right child if isLeft = 0. The list contains every parent-child relation of the tree exactly once and nothing else, and the edges form a single valid binary tree (it has at least two nodes). The root is not named: it is the one node that is never a child.

Return the tree in level-order encoding.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed (or returned) as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree below: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For descriptions = [[20, 15, 1], [20, 17, 0], [50, 20, 1], [50, 80, 0], [80, 19, 1]] the root is 50 with children 20 (left) and 80 (right); node 20 has children 15 and 17, and node 80 has the single left child 19. The answer is [50, 20, 80, 15, 17, 19].
constraints: 0 ≤ parent, child ≤ 10,000; the node values are distinct
The edges describe exactly one valid binary tree (no node has two left or two right children, no cycles, one root)
hints: Which node is the root? Think about which values appear as a parent but never as a child.
Store for every parent its left child and its right child in dictionaries. Then you can move downward from any node in O(1).
After finding the root, run a level-order traversal using the dictionaries (a missing entry means -1), and trim the trailing -1s.
editorial: First pass over the edges: record the left or right child of each parent in two dictionaries, and collect the set of all parents and the set of all children. The root is the single value that is in the parents but not in the children. All other nodes have exactly one parent, so nothing else can be a candidate.

Then run a breadth-first traversal from the root. For a node x the entries to append for its children are left.get(x, -1) and right.get(x, -1), and -1 entries do not get expanded. The tail of -1 values is trimmed at the end. Everything is linear in the number of edges, and the input order of the edges is irrelevant.
